ecom-b1-product-descriptions-that-sell.q: The AI wants to add a claim like "clinically proven" that isn't backed by any fact you supplied. What should the prompt make it do instead?
options: Include the claim anyway since it sounds persuasive
Put it in a separate "needs a source" list instead of the main copy
Delete the whole product description and start over
Let it slide since customers rarely check advertising claims
ecom-b1-product-descriptions-that-sell.why: The "needs a source" list catches plausible-sounding claims the model wants to add on its own, so you see exactly what to verify or cut before publishing.

ecom-b1-product-descriptions-that-sell.q: Why should the description lead with the buyer's problem instead of the product name?
options: It's required by Amazon's search algorithm
Shoppers skim for "is this for me" before reading features, which is what actually improves conversion
Product names are always too long to lead with
It reduces the overall word count
ecom-b1-product-descriptions-that-sell.why: Leading with the buyer's problem matches how shoppers actually read a listing, which is why it converts better than opening with a brand or product name.

ecom-b1-product-descriptions-that-sell.q: What's the single biggest risk in AI-written product copy that this lesson warns about?
options: Using too few bullet points
Letting the AI fill blank spec fields with plausible-sounding but invented numbers
Writing in too warm a tone
Keeping the description under 200 words
ecom-b1-product-descriptions-that-sell.why: Restricting the AI to only the facts you supply is the core guardrail against hallucinated specs, which is the single biggest risk in AI-written product copy.

ecom-b2-ad-copy-variants-for-testing.q: You ask for "10 ad variations" without naming distinct angles. What's the likely result?
options: 10 genuinely distinct hypotheses ready for a meaningful A/B test
10 rewordings of essentially the same idea, telling you nothing useful about what moves your audience
The AI will refuse the request as too vague
Exactly 10 platform-specific formats
ecom-b2-ad-copy-variants-for-testing.why: Asking for variations without naming structured angles almost always produces near-duplicate rewordings of one idea rather than genuinely different tests.

ecom-b2-ad-copy-variants-for-testing.q: Why label each ad variant with the specific angle it tests (price, urgency, social proof, etc.)?
options: It's required by every ad platform's upload format
It makes it possible to trace test results back to a hypothesis, instead of just knowing which wording won with no idea why
It automatically shortens each variant
It increases click-through rate on its own
ecom-b2-ad-copy-variants-for-testing.why: Labeling by angle turns a winning variant into a learning about your audience, rather than just a preferred wording.

ecom-b2-ad-copy-variants-for-testing.q: Which of these should the prompt explicitly ban the AI from doing?
options: Staying within the platform's character limits
Inventing a discount percentage or guarantee that isn't real
Labeling each variant by its tested angle
Writing exactly one variant per angle
ecom-b2-ad-copy-variants-for-testing.why: An invented discount or guarantee can lead to ad rejections and false-advertising exposure, so the prompt must ban adding claims not in the real offer.

ecom-i1-product-lifestyle-photos-ai-imag.q: A store owner wants to use a fully AI-generated image (from ChatGPT or Gemini) as their Amazon primary listing photo. What's wrong with this?
options: Nothing — AI images are acceptable everywhere on marketplaces
Most marketplaces require the primary listing photo to be an actual photograph of the real item
AI images are always too low-resolution for listings
It violates ChatGPT's and Gemini's terms of service
ecom-i1-product-lifestyle-photos-ai-imag.why: AI-generated imagery belongs in secondary and marketing placements, not the primary listing slot, which platforms require to be a literal photograph.

ecom-i1-product-lifestyle-photos-ai-imag.q: Why upload a reference image of your real product when generating a lifestyle scene with ChatGPT (GPT Image 2) or Gemini (Nano Banana 2)?
options: It's required for the tool to function at all
It anchors the generation so the model doesn't "helpfully" reinvent the product's actual appearance
It makes image generation faster
It removes the need to review the output afterward
ecom-i1-product-lifestyle-photos-ai-imag.why: Anchoring to a real reference image is the key guardrail against the model altering the product's real color, proportions, or features, which becomes a truth-in-advertising problem in paid ads.

ecom-i1-product-lifestyle-photos-ai-imag.q: What should you never ask GPT Image 2 or Nano Banana 2 to render directly into the scene?
options: Multiple variations for comparison
Text or logos, since these suffer from a common garbled-text failure mode in image models
A specific aspect ratio for the destination platform
Lighting and mood descriptions
ecom-i1-product-lifestyle-photos-ai-imag.why: Rendered text and logos are a common failure mode for image models; typography should be added afterward in a design tool instead.

ecom-i2-customer-service-replies-refunds.q: A customer's order is 12 days late and no specific new delivery date is confirmed. What should the AI-drafted reply do?
options: Invent a plausible delivery date to reassure the customer
State the honest facts and, since the resolution isn't fully clear, say so and list what's needed instead of guessing
Promise a full refund regardless of your actual policy
Skip the delay topic and focus only on a general apology
ecom-i2-customer-service-replies-refunds.why: The explicit fallback to say so and list what's needed stops the AI from confidently inventing a resolution when the facts given are incomplete.

ecom-i2-customer-service-replies-refunds.q: Why does the prompt require opening with acknowledgment of the specific issue instead of a generic "sorry for the inconvenience"?
options: Generic apologies are against most platforms' policies
It changes how the reply lands with an already-frustrated customer compared to boilerplate language
It reduces the total word count
It's required for chargeback disputes specifically
ecom-i2-customer-service-replies-refunds.why: Naming the specific issue rather than a generic apology is what actually reads as genuine to a frustrated customer.

ecom-i2-customer-service-replies-refunds.q: What's the core guardrail this lesson emphasizes for refund and complaint replies?
options: Grounding every draft in your real order facts and real policy so it never invents a promise you can't honor
Always offering the maximum possible remedy to prevent complaints
Keeping every reply under 50 words regardless of complexity
Never mentioning specific order details in a reply
ecom-i2-customer-service-replies-refunds.why: The realistic risk with AI-drafted replies is a confidently invented promise — a specific timeline, dollar amount, or exception — that was never actually authorized.

ecom-i3-email-flows-welcome-abandoned-ca.q: A 3-email abandoned-cart flow reads almost identically in all three emails, just with different subject lines. What went wrong?
options: This is correct — repetition reinforces the message
Each email should have a distinct job (e.g., set expectations, build trust, create urgency) — repeating the same message is the most common flow failure
The subject lines should have been identical too
The send timing between the emails was wrong
ecom-i3-email-flows-welcome-abandoned-ca.why: Assigning a distinct job to each email prevents a flow from collapsing into three versions of the same generic message.

ecom-i3-email-flows-welcome-abandoned-ca.q: Why explicitly instruct "do not invent a discount... if I said no discount, do not add one anywhere in the flow"?
options: Discounts are illegal in automated email marketing
Models default to adding urgency with a made-up percentage off even when never asked, which can cost real margin
It's purely a formatting requirement
It shortens the overall email flow
ecom-i3-email-flows-welcome-abandoned-ca.why: Without this guardrail, an AI-drafted flow can silently add a discount that was never authorized, costing real margin if shipped unreviewed.

ecom-i3-email-flows-welcome-abandoned-ca.q: Before turning a new automated flow on for real customers, what must happen?
options: Load it directly into the platform and monitor results
Test-trigger the full flow end to end yourself first
Publish it and only check open rates afterward
Skip review since AI-generated copy reads confidently
ecom-i3-email-flows-welcome-abandoned-ca.why: Testing the flow by triggering it yourself is what catches broken timing, links, or copy issues before real customers ever see it.

ecom-a1-automate-recurring-store-content.q: You're designing an automation that auto-drafts a description whenever a new SKU is added. What's the mandatory checkpoint before anything publishes?
options: An automated spellcheck step
A human approval step before anything publishes or sends
A/B testing the copy automatically
A 24-hour delay before publishing
ecom-a1-automate-recurring-store-content.why: Unreviewed AI output publishing directly to customers is the realistic failure mode, so a mandatory human approval checkpoint is the core safety guardrail.

ecom-a1-automate-recurring-store-content.q: Why scope the first automation to one recurring task instead of the whole content calendar at once?
options: Claude and ChatGPT can only handle one instruction at a time
It prevents building a fragile multi-step system before you know the pattern actually works
It's required by Claude's and ChatGPT's pricing tiers
One task uses less AI compute
ecom-a1-automate-recurring-store-content.why: Proving out one task first avoids building an elaborate, fragile automation before validating that the basic pattern is reliable.

ecom-a1-automate-recurring-store-content.q: What happens if the AI drafting step is built around fields that aren't reliably present at trigger time (e.g., missing spec fields on a new product)?
options: It automatically skips that product with no issue
It causes thin or broken drafts
The whole automation stops working
It has no effect since AI fills gaps intelligently
ecom-a1-automate-recurring-store-content.why: Prompt templates built around fields that aren't always populated at trigger time produce thin or broken drafts, which is why the design should flag or route around missing data.

cs-b1-rewrite-difficult-reply-firm-kind-.q: A refund is genuinely denied, but the rewritten reply hedges so much that the customer could reasonably think it's negotiable. What went wrong?
options: The reply was too firm and needs softening
The decision wasn't stated clearly within the first two sentences, implying flexibility that doesn't exist
The reply was too short overall
The customer's concern wasn't acknowledged
cs-b1-rewrite-difficult-reply-firm-kind-.why: Burying a firm "no" under too much hedging is the most common failure in written support replies, and it produces more follow-up tickets, not fewer.

cs-b1-rewrite-difficult-reply-firm-kind-.q: Why does the prompt separate "acknowledge the customer's frustration" from "apologize for the decision itself"?
options: They mean the same thing so it doesn't matter
It keeps empathy genuine without implying the company did something wrong when the decision was actually correct
Apologies are against most companies' written policy
It shortens the overall reply
cs-b1-rewrite-difficult-reply-firm-kind-.why: Apologizing for a correct decision undermines your own policy, while acknowledging frustration without apologizing keeps the reply both honest and kind.

cs-b1-rewrite-difficult-reply-firm-kind-.q: What's a common mistake this lesson warns against?
options: Stating the actual decision clearly in the opening
Accepting an invented workaround or discount the AI added even though none was authorized
Reading the reply once more as if you were the customer before sending
Keeping the real decision unchanged from what you supplied
cs-b1-rewrite-difficult-reply-firm-kind-.why: The AI may manufacture a plausible workaround or discount that oversteps your actual authority, so any added exception must be checked against what was truly authorized.

cs-b2-macro-library-from-real-tickets.q: The AI rewrites your team's proven, real reply into more polished, generic customer-service language. Is this an improvement?
options: Yes, always improve the wording for professionalism
No — this strips out the tone that's already proven to work with your customers, replacing it with boilerplate
Yes, since generic wording reduces the chance of errors
It doesn't matter as long as the facts stay accurate
cs-b2-macro-library-from-real-tickets.why: The instruction to preserve wording and structure protects tone that's already proven effective instead of defaulting to generic template language.

cs-b2-macro-library-from-real-tickets.q: Why require specific placeholders like [ORDER #] and [DAYS DELAYED] instead of vague ones like [DETAILS]?
options: Vague placeholders are simply shorter to type
Specific placeholders reduce the risk of an agent sending a macro with a placeholder or stale detail left in it
CRM software requires exact bracket syntax
It makes the overall library file smaller
cs-b2-macro-library-from-real-tickets.why: Vague placeholders are the most common way a macro goes out with an unfilled field or a leftover detail from a previous customer.

cs-b2-macro-library-from-real-tickets.q: How should you start building this macro library?
options: Cover every possible ticket type at once for completeness
Start with 5-8 of your highest-frequency real ticket types
Use only the newest agent's replies as the source
Skip writing a fill-in checklist to save time
cs-b2-macro-library-from-real-tickets.why: Building the whole library at once instead of starting with the highest-frequency types is a common mistake that delays getting real value from the library.

cs-i1-knowledge-base-articles-from-resol.q: A resolved ticket's fix actually depended on the customer also being on an updated app version, though this wasn't stated as a general requirement. How should the KB draft handle this?
options: State the fix as universally true for every customer in this situation
Flag it under a "needs verification" note instead of stating it as generally true fact
Omit the article entirely since it's unclear
Publish immediately since it worked for one customer
cs-i1-knowledge-base-articles-from-resol.why: A resolved ticket is evidence for one case, not proof the same steps work for every customer, so uncertain generalizations must be flagged, not stated as fact.

cs-i1-knowledge-base-articles-from-resol.q: Why is a human technical review required before publishing a KB article drafted from one ticket?
options: It's a formality with no real risk involved
A resolved ticket only proves the fix worked for one case, not that it generalizes to every customer
AI-drafted articles are always factually wrong
Search engines require human-authored content
cs-i1-knowledge-base-articles-from-resol.why: Publishing an unverified 'always do X' step that only worked because of one customer's specific account state can actively mislead future readers.

cs-i1-knowledge-base-articles-from-resol.q: What's a common mistake this lesson warns against?
options: Stripping customer-identifying details before pasting the ticket into the prompt
Publishing a KB article straight from the AI draft without a technical review confirming it holds generally
Including a "when this might not work" section
Phrasing the article title as a real customer search query
cs-i1-knowledge-base-articles-from-resol.why: Skipping the technical review is the primary risk this lesson addresses, since it's what catches whether the resolution actually generalizes.

cs-i2-escalation-summaries-engineers-man.q: The technical summary states a likely root cause that was never actually confirmed in the ticket thread. What's the risk?
options: None — engineers will verify it themselves anyway
It can send debugging in the wrong direction and waste real engineering time
It makes the summary more thorough and useful
It speeds up the resolution process
cs-i2-escalation-summaries-engineers-man.why: A support agent guessing at a technical cause and stating it confidently can misdirect an engineer's investigation, which the prompt explicitly forbids.

cs-i2-escalation-summaries-engineers-man.q: Why generate both the technical and manager summaries from the exact same source facts in one pass?
options: It's simply faster to type once
It keeps the two summaries from drifting into inconsistent stories as the escalation gets retold
Managers and engineers read the identical document anyway
It reduces the total word count needed
cs-i2-escalation-summaries-engineers-man.why: Generating both from the same facts prevents the technical and manager versions of the story from contradicting each other over time.

cs-i2-escalation-summaries-engineers-man.q: A reproduction detail (like the browser used) wasn't captured in the thread. What should the technical summary do?
options: Guess the most common browser to keep the summary complete
Flag it explicitly as "missing — need to obtain"
Omit any mention of reproduction steps entirely
Leave it out and note nothing about it
cs-i2-escalation-summaries-engineers-man.why: Flagging missing reproduction details turns a gap into an action item instead of a silent hole in the report.

cs-i3-tone-consistency-across-support-te.q: Instead of grounding the tone guide in your team's own real replies, you ask for generic customer-service tone advice. What's the problem?
options: Nothing — generic advice generalizes better across teams
It produces something nobody actually references since it isn't concrete or specific to how your team actually writes
Generic advice is inherently more accurate
It takes longer for the AI to generate
cs-i3-tone-consistency-across-support-te.why: Grounding the guide in real examples is what makes it something agents can pattern-match against, instead of another set of abstract adjectives everyone interprets differently.

cs-i3-tone-consistency-across-support-te.q: Why require a real example next to every do/don't point in the tone guide?
options: It's purely a formatting preference
It's the mechanism that keeps the guide concrete instead of abstract adjectives like "be friendly"
Examples are legally required in HR documentation
It shortens the overall checklist
cs-i3-tone-consistency-across-support-te.why: Abstract adjectives on their own get interpreted differently by every agent; a concrete example next to each point removes that ambiguity.

cs-i3-tone-consistency-across-support-te.q: How should the pre-send checklist be used after the team has been trained on it?
options: Only during new-hire onboarding
To periodically spot-check real sent replies, not just new drafts
Never revisited once the guide is written
Only applied to escalation tickets
cs-i3-tone-consistency-across-support-te.why: Using the checklist only for training misses how tone naturally drifts over time even after everyone has already been trained on the guide.

cs-a1-triage-workflows-ai-assistance-hum.q: The AI classifier has low confidence on an ambiguous incoming ticket. What should the workflow do by default?
options: Force-classify it into the AI's best-guess category anyway
Route it to a human review queue by default rather than guessing
Auto-close it since it's ambiguous
Delete it to keep the queue clean
cs-a1-triage-workflows-ai-assistance-hum.why: The low-confidence-routes-to-human default rule keeps genuinely uncertain cases from being silently mishandled.

cs-a1-triage-workflows-ai-assistance-hum.q: Why must a VIP-tagged or possible churn/legal-risk ticket always go to a human, regardless of AI confidence level?
options: VIP tickets simply take longer to process either way
These are exactly the high-stakes cases where an unnoticed auto-routing or auto-closing error causes real damage
Every helpdesk platform legally requires this
AI models cannot technically read account tags
cs-a1-triage-workflows-ai-assistance-hum.why: The realistic failure mode in support automation is a high-stakes, ambiguous ticket being auto-handled with nobody noticing until real damage is done.

cs-a1-triage-workflows-ai-assistance-hum.q: What's a common mistake to avoid when rolling out this triage workflow?
options: Testing the AI's classification against a batch of past tickets before going live
Letting the AI auto-close or auto-resolve tickets in the first version instead of keeping resolution and closing fully human
Defining an explicit low-confidence fallback rule
Listing your real ticket categories exactly as your team currently uses them
cs-a1-triage-workflows-ai-assistance-hum.why: This workflow is designed for classification and routing only — resolution and closing must stay human, especially in the first version.
